stem: To what extent was the failure of constitutional methods the main reason why nationalists in Zimbabwe turned to armed struggle in the 1960s?

points.description: Constitutional methods: Congress, the NDP and ZAPU used rallies, petitions, boycotts and negotiation, but the 1961 constitution offered only 15 of 65 seats and no guaranteed majority
Repression closed legal politics: bans of 1959, 1961, 1962 and 1964, states of emergency, detention of leaders and the Law and Order (Maintenance) Act
Government refusal to negotiate under the Rhodesian Front (1962 and 1964) and UDI in 1965
Underlying grievances: the Land Apportionment Act, crowded reserves, discrimination and the limited franchise
Decolonisation in Africa: independence of Ghana, Tanganyika, Zambia and Malawi, bases and help from Tanzania and Zambia, training in China and the Soviet bloc
Nationalist divisions: the split of 1963 and rivalry between ZAPU and ZANU, and the link to the memory of 1896-97
Evaluation: weighing constitutional failure against repression, grievances and the international setting, with a supported judgement

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The failure of constitutional methods was the most important immediate reason why nationalists turned to armed struggle, but it cannot be separated from repression, from deep grievances and from the wider African setting. A judgement must show how these causes fitted together.

The underlying grievances were long-standing. The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 gave the best land to whites and left most Africans crowded in reserves, and later laws such as the Land Husbandry Act of 1951 added to the pressure. Africans faced discrimination in jobs, wages, education and public life, and the franchise was limited by qualifications so that almost all voters were white. These grievances explain why Africans wanted change, and they also linked the nationalist cause to the risings of 1896-97. But they existed for decades before the 1960s without causing a guerrilla war. They show what Africans wanted, not why armed struggle began when it did.

Constitutional methods were tried first and for several years. The Southern Rhodesia African National Congress of 1957, the National Democratic Party of 1960 and ZAPU of 1961 held rallies, organised strikes and boycotts, petitioned and negotiated. The most important test was the constitutional conference of 1961. The proposals gave Africans 15 of 65 seats on a system of two voters' rolls, with no guarantee of a majority, and they were approved in a referendum in which almost only whites could vote. Nationalist leaders first seemed to accept and then rejected the terms, which showed both the divisions among them and how little the proposals offered. When the best that peaceful politics could win was a minority of seats, the case for other methods grew stronger.

Repression turned that disappointment into a decision. Congress was banned in 1959 under a state of emergency; the NDP was banned in 1961 and ZAPU in 1962; and in August 1964 ZANU and the People's Caretaker Council were banned and their leaders detained, in many cases for ten years. Laws such as the Law and Order (Maintenance) Act allowed detention without trial. Each ban removed a legal route and pushed leaders and supporters abroad. The Rhodesian Front, in power from December 1962 and led by Ian Smith from April 1964, refused to discuss majority rule, and the unilateral declaration of independence of 11 November 1965 showed that the white government would not give up power peacefully. After UDI there was no British authority that Africans could appeal to, and British attempts at a settlement, such as the talks on HMS Tiger in 1966, left white control intact.

The wider setting made armed struggle seem both necessary and possible. Ghana became independent in 1957, Tanganyika in 1961, and Zambia and Malawi in 1964; FRELIMO began its war in Mozambique in 1964. These examples showed that colonial rule could end, and the independent states of Zambia and Tanzania offered bases, while China, the Soviet Union and their allies provided training and weapons to ZANU and ZAPU respectively. Without this support a guerrilla war would have been impossible, although it does not explain why nationalists wanted one.

The divisions among the nationalists also mattered. The split of 1963 into ZAPU and ZANU, with its violence in the townships, weakened peaceful politics and gave the government an excuse for tougher action. At the same time, rivalry encouraged each party to prove itself by taking up the fight. Historians disagree about the weight of leadership, strategy and personal rivalry in the split, but most accept that it contributed to the atmosphere in which armed struggle began.

Weighing these causes, I conclude that the failure of constitutional methods was the central reason, but only when linked to repression and the refusal to negotiate. Failure alone might have led to continued protest; it was the closing of every legal route by bans and detention, and then by UDI, that made violence seem the only choice. The deep grievances, above all over land, provided the motive and the popular support that later made the war possible, and decolonisation provided the means. So the main reason was the combination of failed constitutional methods and repression, resting on grievances that no peaceful method had been able to remedy. The military phase of 1966-72 failed, but the decision to fight had been made by the events of the early 1960s.

stem: Assess the view that independence in 1980 was won by the armed struggle rather than by negotiation.

points.description: The armed struggle from 1972: Altena Farm, mobilisation of villagers through pungwes and mediums, Mozambique as base
Pressure on Rhodesia by 1978-79: spread of the war, white emigration, economic strain, sanctions, call-ups
The failures of peaceful attempts before the war's pressure grew: HMS Tiger, Fearless, Pearce, Geneva, and the internal settlement that did not end the war
Negotiation: the Commonwealth meeting at Lusaka, the Frontline States, Lancaster House terms, the ceasefire and the supervised election
Compromises made at Lancaster House: reserved white seats, the property clause and the land question
Role of other factors: sanctions, Britain's and the United States' diplomacy, South Africa's changing stance
Evaluation: relationship between the war and the talks, with a supported judgement

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Independence in 1980 cannot be explained by armed struggle alone or by negotiation alone. The war created the pressure that made a settlement necessary, but the settlement itself was reached by negotiation at Lancaster House and shaped by outside powers and compromises. I will argue that the armed struggle was the main force, because without it no settlement acceptable to the nationalists would have been offered, but that negotiation determined how and on what terms independence came.

The armed struggle changed after 1972. In the 1960s the campaigns at Chinhoyi, Wankie and Sipolilo had been defeated, because the fighters lacked the support of villagers. From the attack at Altena Farm on 21 December 1972, ZANLA fighters instead worked first with the rural people, using pungwe meetings, spirit mediums and young messengers called mujibas and chimbwidos, and used Mozambique as a base. After Mozambique became independent in 1975 and closed its border to Rhodesia in 1976, the war spread across the eastern and northern parts of the country, while ZIPRA operated from Zambia. The Rhodesian government responded with protected villages, special forces and raids into neighbouring states, but these measures angered villagers and failed to stop recruitment.

By 1978-79 the pressure on Rhodesia was severe. Large areas of the countryside were out of government control after dark, white emigration had risen, the economy was strained by the cost of the war and by sanctions in force since 1965-66, and the reservists on whom the army depended were called up for long periods. Estimates of the number killed range from about 20,000 to 30,000 or more. These facts show that the armed struggle had made the old order unsustainable. They also explain why earlier peaceful attempts had failed while the white government felt confident: the talks on HMS Tiger in 1966 and HMS Fearless in 1968, the Pearce Commission of 1972, the Victoria Falls Conference of 1975 and Geneva in 1976 all broke down when Smith's government believed it could keep control. The internal settlement of March 1978, which left whites in charge of the army, police and courts, did not end the war, because the Patriotic Front fought on and no foreign government recognised it. In this sense the war was what made negotiation work.

Yet the settlement was not a direct result of the war. The Commonwealth meeting at Lusaka in August 1979 persuaded the new British prime minister, Margaret Thatcher, to call a conference of all parties rather than recognise Bishop Muzorewa's government. The Frontline States, especially Mozambique under Samora Machel and Zambia under Kenneth Kaunda, pressed the Patriotic Front to compromise, because their own countries were suffering from Rhodesian raids and from the war's costs. At Lancaster House, chaired by Lord Carrington from 10 September to 21 December 1979, the Patriotic Front accepted a constitution that reserved 20 of 100 seats for whites for seven years and protected property for ten years, leaving land to a willing seller, willing buyer approach. These were concessions that a movement certain of military victory might not have made. The ceasefire, the British governor Lord Soames, and the elections of February 1980 were all products of negotiation.

Other factors also contributed. Sanctions and the loss of Mozambique as a friendly neighbour weakened Rhodesia. South Africa, which had helped Rhodesia, became less willing to support a long war and favoured a settlement that would produce a government it could live with. American and British diplomacy provided the framework, as in the Anglo-American proposals of 1977.

Weighing the two, I conclude that the armed struggle was the main reason independence came when it did, since it made the Rhodesian state's position impossible and forced the British, the Frontline States and the white government to seek a settlement. However, negotiation was essential to how independence came: it prevented a longer war, secured international recognition and the lifting of sanctions, and gave the nationalists a fair election, which ZANU (PF) won with 57 of the 80 common-roll seats. It also set limits, on land, property and the white seats, that shaped the next decades. Independence was therefore won by the war, but achieved through negotiation.

stem: Examine the political challenges faced by the government of Zimbabwe between 1980 and 1990 and assess how far they were overcome.

points.description: Reconciliation: the government of national unity, white and PF-ZAPU ministers, the retention of civil servants, and the Lancaster House limits
Integration of the armies: ZANLA, ZIPRA and Rhodesian units, clashes at Entumbane in 1980 and 1981
Rivalry between ZANU (PF) and PF-ZAPU: arms caches, Nkomo's dismissal in 1982, dissident activity
The disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands, 1982-87: the Fifth Brigade, civilian deaths (estimates disputed), different accounts
The Unity Accord of 22 December 1987 and its terms: merged party, amnesty, executive presidency
Other political developments: the end of white seats, elections of 1985 and 1990, the one-party debate
Evaluation: how far challenges were overcome, with a supported judgement that acknowledges costs and different views

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The government that took office in March 1980 faced three main political challenges: building a united nation after a long war and a divided colonial society, merging three armies, and managing rivalry between the two nationalist parties. By 1990 the first had been largely met, the second only after serious violence, and the third by the Unity Accord of 1987, which ended the fighting but at a cost that is still debated.

The first challenge was reconciliation. On taking office Robert Mugabe urged Zimbabweans to forgive the past. He formed a government that included Joshua Nkomo and other PF-ZAPU members, with Nkomo as Minister of Home Affairs, and two white ministers. White civil servants, judges and officers were kept in their posts, and the Lancaster House terms on land and property were accepted. These policies preserved skills and avoided the economic collapse that occurred in some other countries at independence, and they were widely praised abroad. Critics argue that they also delayed land reform and left the economic structures of the colonial period largely unchanged, and that little was done for the victims of the war.

The second challenge was the merging of three armies: ZANLA, ZIPRA and the former Rhodesian forces. A British military training team helped to create the new Zimbabwe National Army. But the former guerrillas of the two nationalist armies distrusted each other, and in November 1980 and February 1981 there were serious clashes between ZIPRA and ZANLA units at Entumbane, near Bulawayo. These events showed that the rivalry of the war, and the split between ZAPU and ZANU in 1963, had not ended with independence.

The third challenge was the confrontation between ZANU (PF), which had won 57 of the 80 common-roll seats in 1980, and PF-ZAPU, which had won 20. In early 1982 the government announced the discovery of arms caches on PF-ZAPU properties and, in February, dismissed Nkomo and other PF-ZAPU ministers from the cabinet. Armed dissidents, some of them former ZIPRA soldiers and according to reports some with South African support, began attacks in Matabeleland. In January 1983 the government deployed the Fifth Brigade, a unit trained by North Korean instructors, in Matabeleland North and later in the south. Reports by the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace and by survivors record many killings and other abuses against civilians, as well as killings by dissidents. Estimates of the civilian dead, such as the figure of about 20,000 in a 1997 report, are disputed and the true number is not known. The government at the time described its actions as a response to armed dissidents; others describe a campaign against civilians. Both accounts need to be stated, and later official statements have recognised that wrongs were done. The events left a legacy of grievance in Matabeleland and the Midlands that remains a matter of public debate.

The Unity Accord of 22 December 1987 resolved the conflict between the two parties. ZANU (PF) and PF-ZAPU merged under the name ZANU (PF), Mugabe became the first executive president on 31 December 1987, with provision for two vice-presidents, and an amnesty followed for dissidents in 1988. The 20 white seats had already been abolished earlier in 1987. The Accord ended the dissident conflict and gave the country political stability. However, it also created a dominant-party system, with little room for opposition, and many people in the affected regions felt that their grievances were not addressed. The elections of 1990, in which ZANU (PF) won 117 of 120 elected seats, and the rejection by the party in 1991 of a proposal for a formal one-party state, showed both the dominance of the ruling party and some limits to it.

Assessing how far the challenges were overcome, I conclude that reconciliation between races was largely successful, since whites remained and the economy kept its skills, though at the cost of delaying changes in land. The integration of armies and the rivalry between the parties were overcome only after violence which cost many lives, and by the merger of parties rather than by agreement to compete peacefully. The settlement of 1987 was a political success in ending the war within the country, yet it left unresolved questions about acknowledgement and justice for victims, and it narrowed political competition. The government overcame the immediate challenges to its survival, but not all of the deeper ones, and historians and Zimbabweans differ in the weight they give to stability and to its price.

stem: Assess the effects of the partition of Africa on Africa and on Europe.

points.description: Process: the Berlin Conference (1884-85) set rules of effective occupation and notification; partition by treaties such as the Anglo-German agreement of 1890 and by conquest
Africa: loss of sovereignty, treaties treated as transfers of power, absence of Africans at Berlin
Africa: artificial borders dividing peoples (Somali, Kongo, Ewe) and joining rivals, with lasting effects
Africa: exploitation, with taxes, forced labour and cash crops, and the Congo Free State as the worst case

Evaluation: comparison of the effects on Africa and Europe and a supported judgement on which were greater

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The partition of Africa between about 1880 and 1900 transformed Africa far more deeply than Europe, although it also affected Europe by adding to the rivalries that led to war in 1914. To assess the effects I will take Africa first, then Europe, and then compare them.

The process itself shaped the effects. The Berlin Conference, which met from November 1884 to February 1885 under Bismarck, set rules for claiming coastal territory: effective occupation and notification to other powers. It also recognised Leopold II's claim to the Congo. No African ruler attended. The conference did not draw the map, which was drawn afterwards by treaties between Europeans, such as the Anglo-German agreement of 1890 and the Anglo-Portuguese treaty of 1891, by treaties with African rulers, and by conquest. The rules encouraged a rush to place posts and sign treaties before rivals did.

For Africa, the first effect was the loss of sovereignty. States that had traded and made treaties as equals found themselves under foreign rule, and treaties that rulers had understood as friendship or trade were treated by Europeans as transfers of power. Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia were the only exceptions. The second effect was the creation of artificial borders. Boundaries were drawn on maps by officials who knew little of the ground, dividing peoples such as the Somali, the Kongo and the Ewe among several colonies and joining others with different histories in one. Many of these boundaries survived independence and became a cause of later disputes. A third effect was economic and social exploitation. Colonies were run for the benefit of the European rulers, through taxes that forced people into wage work or cash cropping, forced labour for roads and plantations, and the seizure of land in settler colonies. The worst example was the Congo Free State, where forced labour for rubber caused great suffering until international protest led Belgium to take it over in 1908.

Africans did not accept these changes passively. Resistance took many forms, from the armed resistance of Samori Touré, of the Ndebele and Shona in 1896-97 and of the many peoples of the Maji Maji rising in 1905-07, to the diplomacy of Menelik II, who kept Ethiopia independent by combining arms with letters to the powers. Most armed resistance was defeated, often with great loss of life, because Europeans had machine guns, quinine and the support of other Africans, but resistance forced colonial states to adopt compromises and left traditions that later nationalists drew on.

For Europe the effects were different. The partition gave the powers empires, markets, raw materials and national pride, and it strengthened ideas of racial superiority which were used to justify colonial rule. It also reduced the risk of immediate war over Africa, since the powers agreed rules and compromises. But the rivalry continued. Britain and France came close to war at Fashoda in 1898, before settling their disputes in the Entente Cordiale of 1904, and Germany's challenge to France in Morocco in the crises of 1905 and 1911 raised tension between the great powers. These crises did not cause the war of 1914, but they deepened mistrust and helped to form the alliances that made a European war larger when it came.

Comparing the two, the effects on Africa were far greater and longer lasting. For Africans the partition meant the loss of independence, new borders and political systems, economic change and, in many places, violence and exploitation, with consequences that lasted until independence and beyond. For Europe the partition brought gains in wealth and prestige for some groups and costs in rivalry for the state system, but the effects were secondary to causes closer to home, such as the alliance system and nationalism in the Balkans. Historians stress different consequences, some emphasising the economic gains and others the rivalries, but most accept that Africa bore the main burden.

I conclude that the partition was above all a transformation of Africa, with effects on sovereignty, borders and the economy that shaped the continent's history for a century, while for Europe it was an addition to existing tensions rather than a turning point.

stem: Why did Ethiopia succeed in resisting European conquest while the Maji Maji uprising in German East Africa failed? To what extent do differences in leadership explain the contrast?

points.description: Ethiopia: Menelik II united the rases and the church, mobilised a large army and used diplomacy with France, Russia and Britain
Ethiopia: modern rifles and artillery bought from Europe; railway and telegraph; the state's long history
Italian weaknesses: poor maps and intelligence, divided columns, pressure from Rome; the defeat at Adwa on 1 March 1896 and the Treaty of Addis Ababa
Maji Maji: religious leadership of Kinjikitile and the maji medicine united many peoples but he was hanged in August 1905 and there was no central command
Maji Maji: few modern weapons, belief in protection against bullets, German machine guns, reinforcements, scorched earth and famine
Other differences: an existing state against a loose alliance of peoples; 1896 against 1905; aims of defending a state against expelling rulers; different European opponents

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Ethiopia and the Maji Maji peoples both resisted European conquest in the period of the Scramble, but Ethiopia kept its independence after the victory at Adwa in 1896 while the Maji Maji rising of 1905-07 was crushed with enormous loss of life. Differences in leadership were important, but they were part of wider differences in organisation, weapons and the opponent. I will argue that leadership matters most when it is understood as the ability of a state to prepare, rather than as the qualities of one man.

Ethiopia's resistance was led by an experienced ruler of an established state. Menelik II, who became emperor in 1889, united the regional nobles, the rases, and the church around the defence of an independent Christian kingdom. He built a new capital at Addis Ababa, raised revenue, and used it to buy modern rifles and artillery from France, Russia and Italy itself. He also used diplomacy. When Italy claimed that the Treaty of Wuchale of 1889 made Ethiopia a protectorate, because the Italian text of Article 17 said Menelik agreed to use Italy for his dealings with the powers, whereas the Amharic text said he could, he denounced the treaty in 1893 and wrote to the European powers to assert Ethiopia's independence, playing them off against each other. When Italy invaded in 1895, Menelik called out an army of the whole country. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 an Ethiopian force of tens of thousands defeated an Italian army of about 17,000 under General Baratieri, whose maps were poor, whose columns were divided, and who was under pressure from the Italian government to win. The Treaty of Addis Ababa in October 1896 recognised Ethiopian independence.

The Maji Maji uprising was a different kind of movement. It arose from grievances against German rule in southern German East Africa: forced cotton growing, a cash tax, forced labour and abuse by officials called akidas. Many peoples, with few earlier links, joined it after Kinjikitile Ngwale, a spirit medium, taught that the maji, a medicine of water, would turn German bullets to water. The religious leadership gave courage and unity and spread the rising across a wide area within weeks in July 1905. But Kinjikitile was hanged in August 1905, the leadership was local and scattered, and there was no central command or common plan. The rebels had few modern weapons, and the belief that the medicine would protect them led them to charge against machine guns. Governor von Götzen obtained reinforcements and the Germans pursued a scorched-earth policy, burning villages and crops, which caused a famine. By 1907 the rising was over. Estimates of the dead range from about 75,000 to well over 200,000, mostly from famine and disease.

Leadership therefore explains part of the contrast. Menelik had the authority of an emperor, the resources of a state, a plan and the ability to keep nobles together, while the Maji Maji leaders had spiritual authority without a state organisation. But other differences were as important. The first was weapons: Ethiopia's army was equipped with modern firearms, the Maji Maji fighters were not. The second was the organisation of the society: Ethiopia was an old state with taxes, an army and a capital, while the peoples of the south of German East Africa were politically separate and joined together only for a short time. The third was the opponent. Italy in 1896 had a small colonial army, divided leaders and a weak political position at home, while Germany in 1905, though it was surprised, could bring in machine guns and troops from elsewhere and had the means to wage a war of starvation. The fourth was aim: Menelik was defending an existing state and could accept a settlement, while the rebels sought to remove German rule from all the land.

Chance and timing also played a part. Italian mistakes at Adwa might not have been repeated, and the Germans' failure to anticipate the rising in July 1905 might not have mattered had the rebels been better armed.

I conclude that leadership was an important cause of the contrast, but not the main one if it is understood only as the qualities of a person. Menelik's success depended on the state he led and the weapons it had bought; the Maji Maji failure rested on the lack of both. The best explanation is a combination of unity and organisation, weapons, and the relative weakness of the opponent, in which Menelik's leadership was the way those advantages were used.
